fetched_contents.text: Pyrolysis-GC-MS | Pyrolysis Gas Chromatography Pyrolysis Gas Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (Pyro-GC-MS) Home » Our Techniques » Mass Spectrometry » Pyro-GC-MS Pyrolysis Gas Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (Pyrolysis-GC-MS) is an analytical tool used to characterize a wide variety of polymers and composite materials that cannot be analyzed using traditional GC-MS. The fundamental concept of Pyrolysis-GC-MS is not complicated but highly sensitive. A sample is introduced to a heated environment and is broken down into smaller stable fragments/components (aka pyrolyzates) for analysis. The pyrolyzates are then chromatographically separated in the same manner as traditional GC-MS. Similar to traditional GC-MS, the fragments are separated utilizing a compound’s intrinsic affinity for a “stationary phase” (solid support with specialized coating). Once the pyrolyzates are separated, the data is analyzed by highly skilled scientists who can deconvolute and interpret the data and subsequently provide useful information and insight on the original material. In order to conduct a thorough investigation, the Pyrolysis temperature program must be set up in a very specific way. When a sample is introduced into the Pyrolysis unit, it is instantly heated from ambient to the desired temperature in an inert atmosphere. This rapid heating provides reproducible results. If additional tests are needed, the test sample is cooled in an inert atmosphere to room temperature and the Pyrolysis unit is reprogrammed. Several different experiments can be performed and they are explained below. Types of Pyrolysis-GC-MS Analyses * A Single Shot Pyrolysis-GC-MS: The single shot is run at a single temperature, normally >500°C (dependent on the material being examined). The temperature of the sample is rapidly increased at a temperature rate <20 msec to break bonds. This is done in order to characterize the original sample. * A Double Shot Pyrolysis: This is normally run at both low (80-350°C) and high temperatures (500-800°C). The lower temperature analysis is known as a thermal desorption step. This step can be used to examine low molecular weight components (monomers, oligomers, etc.), additives and residual solvents. The higher temperatures allow for the total fragmentation of the higher molecular weight items such as the crosslinked material or the entire polymer backbone. * Evolved Gas Analysis (EGA): This is run by dropping the sample into the Pyrolysis unit set at a low temperature. The furnace is then increased to a high temperature at a set ramp rate. The components that are off-gassed/evolved from the sample are then examined. This testing is done in order to identify the temperature range for the desired component. The Pyrolysis-GC-MS can then be set up the desired temperature range for a more in-depth study of the identified compound. As a side note, Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA) can also be used to aid in the determination of the temperature analysis profile for Pyrolysis-GC-MS. * Low Temperature (normally considered <350°C) Thermal Desorption: This testing would be done for products where additives, residual solvents or other off-gassed components are desired but the polymer identification is not needed. * Reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS: There are certain classes of compounds, for example polyesters, that have complex Pyrolysis mixtures (i.e. many degradation products, etc.). These complex mixtures make the interpretation of the data difficult, if not impossible. When a derivatization technique is utilized, a chemical reaction occurs while the sample is in the Pyrolysis chamber, allowing for a much easier interpretation of the derivatized products. * Heart Cut-EGA GC-MS (HC-EGA-GC-MS): This method is useful when looking for specific components in a highly complex matrix or when the full composition of a complex system is desired. Heart-Cut Pyrolysis involves using the EGA technique to isolate the desired elution times (i.e. zones). The instrument is then programmed to isolate each specified zone identified by EGA. Each zone is then individually analyzed. This technique allows for the examination of regions that might contain multiple components under one peak but are not obvious during the regular Pyrolysis GC-MS analysis. While extremely useful, this technique can add to the complexity and amount of time for the analysis. * Quantitative Pyrolysis-GC-MS: This would be done on a component that the amount present could not be determined using another technique. Pyrolysis involves thermal fragmentation of the analytical sample at temperatures of 500–1400 °C. Abstract Even though pyrolysis in combination with gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (Py-GC–MS) is widely used for molecular characterization of wood, its abilities to determine the taxonomy (species), provenance and the nature and intensity of degradation of archaeological woods are hardly explored. We performed principal component analysis (PCA) on Py-GC–MS data of sound woods and shipwreck woods of Pinus sp. and Quercus sp., to identify the impact of diagenesis on pyrolysis fingerprints. It was found that the proportion of most polysaccharide products decreased significantly upon diagenesis with the exception of 3-hydroxy-2-methyl-2-cyclopenten-1-one, which remains relatively well preserved. Furthermore, the guaiacyl lignin products were generally well preserved with the exception of 4-propylguaiacol, the relative contribution of which decreased considerably. New indices are proposed to establish the preservation state of shipwreck wood (shipwreck wood preservation index; SWPI) on the basis of polysaccharides (SWPIPS) and guaiacyl lignin (SWPILG) and syringyl lignin (SWPILS) fingerprints. Stepwise multiple linear regressions analyses applied on FTIR data of the same samples are indicative of the consistency of both techniques and the potential to identify changes in wood chemistry as a result of degradation. Other factors that influence wood composition, such as the differences between soft- and hardwood lignin and sap- and heartwood were also recognized. * Previous * Next Keywords Archaeological wood Diagenesis Multivariate statistics Preservation indices Polysaccharide Lignin Py-GC-MS 1. Introduction One of the main challenges in archaeological research of shipwrecks is the identification of the tree species used as timber and its growing location, i.e. provenance [1], [2]. The microscopic and dendrologic analyses of shipwreck wood have limited capacities to solve these issues, because of the large anatomical variation between woods of different species, individuals of the same species or even different anatomical sections of the same tree [3], [4]. Organic geochemical approaches are beginning to be of significant aid in the analysis of archaeological wood materials [5], [6]. The composition of arboreal wood depends mainly on tree taxonomy and environmental factors of the growing location [7], [8], [9], [10]. For example, lignin of softwood trees (gymnosperms) is composed of guaiacyl units whereas that of hardwood (angiosperms) contains both guaiacyl and syringyl moieties [11], [12], [13]. Latewood production in annual ring is one of the consequences observed due to the environmental factors [7], [8]. After death, the nature and intensity of the degradation processes depends primarily on the storage conditions, which control the availability of oxygen and the composition of the wood-scavengers community [14], [15]. In case of archaeological and historical woods, degradation can often be recognized on the molecular level, even if the morphological appearance remains unaltered [16], [17]. The intensity of degradation depends heavily on storage conditions (e.g. open air storage in buildings, burial in sediments and soils, aerobic/anaerobic conditions, etc.) and time lapse. Numerous studies focused on understanding wood chemical changes (e.g. [18], [19], [20]), showing that archaeological woods are subjected to biological agents such as fungi, bacteria and insects. More specifically, under aerobic conditions fungi are usually the most important decomposers whereas under anaerobic conditions, bacteria are more significant [21], [22], [23]. In archaeological woods, cellulose and hemicellulose are typically more strongly affected than lignin compounds due to bacterial decomposition under anaerobic conditions [17], [24], [25], [26], [27]. Pyrolysis in combination with gas chromatography and mass-spectrometry (Py-GC–MS) is among the most frequently used techniques for wood studies due to its ability to provide details on the molecular structure of lignocellulose [18], [19], [28], [29], [30], [31], [32], [33]. Py-GC–MS uses thermal degradation in an inert atmosphere (pyrolysis) in combination with chromatographic separation and spectrometric identification of pyrolysis products, in order to assess the molecular composition of intractable materials such as synthetic and natural organic polymers. It has been used to characterize lignin in grass, softwood and hardwood according to distinctive features of the phenylpropane units [12], [34], [35], [36], [37]. It can also be used to distinguish species of the same genus, at least in the case of sound wood, such as several white oak species [38]. Py-GC–MS also showed the similarity of the lignin structure in bark and xylem and chemical differences between sapwood and heartwood [39], [40]. This implies that Py-GC–MS has a potential to identify the wood type (species), source (in terms of plant anatomy) and perhaps growing location of archaeological wood when morphological features inhibit identification at the species level [4]. However, there are few studies on the application of Py-GC–MS to archaeological woods. Branch report on practical challenges and trade-offs of derivatisation

Derivatisation in pyrolysis-GC is useful, but it introduces several technical and interpretative trade-offs. A key practical challenge is the risk of side reactions, decomposition, or incomplete conversion during derivatisation. The EAG technical overview notes that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS is used when complex pyrolysis mixtures make interpretation difficult, and it states that a chemical reaction occurs while the sample is in the Pyrolysis chamber, allowing easier interpretation [N3-F2]. This implies that derivatisation can help with interpretation, but it also means the reaction conditions themselves can perturb the sample. The same source also highlights that Pyro-GC-MS is destructive and that non-homogeneous samples might yield variable results [N3-F2]. This variability can be a major limitation, especially when the sample is already complex or degraded.

Cost, time, and complexity are also important trade-offs. Pyrolysis-GC-MS is described as a technique that can reduce sample preparation compared to traditional GC-MS, but the fetch material explicitly states that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS can add to the complexity and amount of time for the analysis [N3-F2]. The same source notes that cryotrapping and heart-cut EGA-GC-MS are useful for highly complex matrices, but they are also more involved and can increase analysis time [N3-F2]. In archaeological wood analysis, this matters because the sample may already be small, fragile, and chemically altered, so any additional protocol burden can reduce feasibility or increase the risk of sample loss or contamination.

Derivatisation can also affect interpretation and artifact authenticity. The main limitation cited in the RSC review of analytical pyrolysis in cultural heritage is that the pyrolysis products must be sufficiently volatile to undergo gas chromatography, and it warns that interpretation can be challenging and time-consuming [N3-R5]. This is relevant because derivatisation may shift the molecular signature of the sample, making it harder to distinguish original wood chemistry from artefacts introduced by the derivatisation step. The EAG overview also notes that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS can simplify interpretation, but it is still a destructive technique [N3-F2]. In archaeological contexts, this raises concerns about whether derivatisation results represent the original material or an altered fingerprint. The N5 evidence on wood preservation also emphasizes that Py-GC-MS fingerprints can be influenced by diagenesis, and that degradation can change the molecular composition of wood [N5-F4]. This means derivatisation may not only alter GC behavior but also obscure or amplify the effects of ancient preservation processes.

Overall, the practical challenges of derivatisation include side reactions, decomposition, incomplete conversion, variability in non-homogeneous samples, and increased complexity and time [N3-F2][N3-R5]. The trade-offs are worth paying when interpretation is difficult, but they also risk introducing artifacts and making the original chemistry harder to validate [N3-F2][N3-R5]. In archaeological wood, these limitations are especially important because the material is often degraded, small, and chemically complex [N5-F4].

Branch report on context-specific archaeological wood analysis needs

In archaeological wood analysis, derivatisation supports identification of wood species or treatment history, but it does so within a highly constrained context. The N5 evidence shows that Py-GC-MS has been used to assess wood species, provenance, and the nature and intensity of degradation, and that principal component analysis (PCA) has been applied to pyrolysis data to characterize different wood samples [N5-F4]. It also highlights that diagenesis can significantly alter wood fingerprints, so the technique is useful but only after accounting for degradation [N5-F4]. This matters because archaeological wood is often difficult to identify morphologically, especially when preservation is poor [N5-F4]. Derivatisation can therefore help by improving separation and detection of compounds that are otherwise obscured by degradation or complexity.

The N2 evidence reinforces the idea that derivatisation can support species-level identification and treatment history. The search result mentions wood species identification using heart-cut pyrolysis-GC-MS and related chemical analysis [N2-R2]. This suggests that derivatisation-like strategies—such as selective separation and enhanced chemical profiling—are important for distinguishing species and possibly detecting preservatives or other treatment-related compounds. The N4 evidence adds that thermal desorption and pyrolysis are used to investigate changes in wood treatment effectiveness, which implies that derivatisation or related preparative steps can help detect preservatives, additives, or treatment residues [N4-R1]. In other words, derivatisation can help archaeologists infer not only what kind of wood was used but also what treatments it underwent, such as preservation or modification.

The effect of derivatisation on sensitivity and specificity is mixed in the evidence provided. On one hand, the EAG overview states that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS can allow easier interpretation of complex mixtures [N3-F2]. On the other hand, the same source warns that non-homogeneous samples can yield variable results, and that Py-GC-MS is destructive [N3-F2]. The RSC review of analytical pyrolysis also notes that interpretation can be challenging and time-consuming [N3-R5]. This means derivatisation may increase sensitivity by reducing complexity and improving peak resolution, but it can also reduce specificity if the derivatisation reaction or subsequent separation alters the molecular identity of the compounds. In archaeological wood, this is especially important because the sample is often degraded and chemically altered, so the signal may not reflect the original material accurately.

Validation of derivatisation results in archaeological contexts requires strong evidence. The N5 evidence explicitly states that Py-GC-MS fingerprints need to be corrected for the molecular signature imposed by diagenesis, and that stepwise multiple linear regression on FTIR data can indicate consistency between techniques [N5-F4]. This implies that validation should compare derivatisation results with other independent analytical methods, such as FTIR, and should account for preservation effects. The N4 evidence also points to sample preparation steps such as filtering and heating, suggesting that reproducibility and method consistency are central to validation [N4-R2]. In practice, this means archaeologists need not only derivatisation results but also controls, repeated runs, and cross-validation with complementary techniques to establish authenticity.

Overall, derivatisation supports archaeological wood analysis by improving separation and detection of species-related and treatment-related compounds [N2-R2][N4-R1]. However, it also changes sensitivity and specificity in ways that depend on the derivatisation chemistry and the preservation state of the sample [N3-F2][N3-R5]. Validation therefore depends on comparison with other analytical methods and careful accounting of degradation and diagenetic effects [N5-F4].

Branch report on what derivatisation does and why it is useful

Derivatisation steps are used primarily to improve volatility or GC compatibility of wood pyrolysis products. The EAG overview states that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS is employed when complex pyrolysis mixtures make interpretation difficult, and that a chemical reaction occurs while the sample is in the Pyrolysis chamber to allow easier interpretation [N3-F2]. This directly supports the idea that derivatisation is used when pyrolysis products are too complex or non-volatile to be well resolved by GC alone. The RSC review of analytical pyrolysis in cultural heritage notes that one limitation of the technique is that pyrolysis products must be sufficiently volatile to undergo gas chromatography [N3-R5]. This reinforces the rationale: derivatisation makes the products more amenable to chromatographic separation.

Derivatisation also enhances separation or detection of specific wood compounds. The same EAG source explains that heart-cut EGA-GC-MS is useful when looking for specific components in highly complex matrices or when the full composition of a complex system is desired [N3-F2]. This indicates that derivatisation can help isolate and detect compounds that would otherwise be buried in a broad pyrolysis fingerprint. The N2 evidence similarly points to heart-cut pyrolysis-GC-MS and chemical analysis for wood identification, suggesting that derivatisation-like strategies can improve detection of species-specific markers [N2-R2]. The N4 evidence adds that thermal desorption followed by pyrolysis can investigate changes in wood treatment effectiveness, implying that derivatisation can help detect preservatives or other treatment-related compounds [N4-R1]. In archaeological wood, this is especially valuable because the sample may contain degraded products, additives, or preservation agents that are difficult to identify otherwise.

Sample-specific benefits for archaeological wood include reduced preparation burden and improved identification potential. The EAG overview says Pyro-GC-MS can reduce sample preparation compared to traditional GC-MS [N3-F2]. This is important for small, fragile, or degraded archaeological samples where handling is limited. The RSC review notes that Py-GC-MS is useful for characterizing natural and synthetic polymers, including wood, and that it can study chemical degradation [N1-F1]. The N5 evidence on archaeological wood preservation shows that Py-GC-MS can be used to assess diagenesis and that PCA can characterize wood samples [N5-F4]. This means derivatisation can help archaeologists distinguish original wood chemistry from degradation products, even when the sample is altered. The N4 evidence also emphasizes that thermal desorption and pyrolysis can improve analysis efficiency and help investigate changes in treatment effectiveness [N4-R1], which aligns with the practical benefit of using derivatisation to extract meaningful information from difficult samples.

In summary, derivatisation improves volatility/GC compatibility, enhances separation and detection of specific wood compounds, and provides sample-specific benefits such as reduced preparation and better identification of species or treatment history [N3-F2][N3-R5][N2-R2][N4-R1]. Its usefulness in archaeological wood analysis comes from making complex pyrolysis fingerprints more interpretable while preserving enough chemical information to infer original material properties [N1-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence points to several common derivatisation types used with pyrolysis products from wood, though the provided material is more general than wood-specific. The most relevant derivatisation types are those that improve volatility and GC compatibility, including silylation, derivatisation in the pyrolysis chamber, and other chemical transformations designed to make pyrolysis products more amenable to chromatography. The EAG overview explicitly states that reactive Pyrolysis-GC-MS involves a chemical reaction while the sample is in the Pyrolysis chamber, allowing easier interpretation of complex mixtures [N3-F2]. This is a broad derivatisation rationale: the reaction alters the molecular structure so the products can be separated more effectively.

The chemical rationale for these derivatisation steps is to modify molecular structure in ways that improve GC behavior. The general GC derivatisation rationale cited in the chemistry resource is that derivatisation is used to convert analytes to chemical forms more compatible with the chromatographic environment [N6-R1]. The same source notes that functional groups commonly derivatized for GC analysis include alcohols, carboxylic acids, amines, and sulfhydryls [N6-R4]. In the context of pyrolysis products, this means derivatisation likely targets polar or non-volatile compounds, adding functional groups that increase volatility, improve solubility, or allow better separation. The EAG overview also states that derivatisation can allow easier interpretation of complex mixtures [N3-F2], which suggests that the chemical modification changes the molecule in a way that reduces peak broadening or co-elution.

The evidence also indicates that derivatisation can mask or alter original wood chemistry. The RSC review notes that interpretation can be challenging and time-consuming, and that pyrolysis products must be sufficiently volatile to undergo gas chromatography [N3-R5]. The N5 evidence on wood preservation adds that Py-GC-MS fingerprints can be influenced by diagenesis, and that degradation can change molecular composition [N5-F4]. This implies that derivatisation may not only improve GC behavior but also distort the original chemical signature, making it harder to distinguish true wood chemistry from artefacts introduced by the derivatisation step. The EAG overview also warns that Py-GC-MS is destructive and that non-homogeneous samples can yield variable results [N3-F2], which is relevant because derivatisation can change the sample in ways that are not easily reversible.

Overall, the common derivatisation types in this context are silylation, derivatisation in the pyrolysis chamber, and other chemical transformations that make pyrolysis products more volatile or compatible with GC [N3-F2][N6-R1]. The chemical rationale is to modify molecular structure to improve volatility, separation, and detection [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, derivatisation can also mask or alter original wood chemistry, making interpretation more difficult and requiring careful validation [N3-R5][N5-F4].

## Main advantages and challenges of using derivatisation in pyrolysis-GC analysis of archaeological wood
